newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey says Iraq gas plan won't breach UN embargo.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says Iraq gas plan won't breach UN embargo.

text.p: Turkey said on Wednesday a plan by Ankara and Baghdad to launch a joint study on the development of gas fields in Iraq and the building of a pipeline would not breach a six-year-old U.N. trade embargo on Iraq.
"We do not think any international institution will object to such studies," Turkish Energy Minister Recai Kutan told reporters after meeting visiting Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed.
"The studies have nothing to do with the U.N. embargo, which has turned into an unfair practice on the Iraqis," he said.
"We are hoping that the embargo will be lifted by the time we have completed the study. So there will not be any obstacle to implementing it," Kutan said.

The United Nations says the embargo, imposed after Baghdad's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, would remain in place until it is fully satisfied Baghdad does not hide any weapons of mass destruction. The world body periodically revises the situation in Iraq to determine whether to lift the embargo.
Iraq was allowed by the U.N. to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine to relieve its people's suffering from the embargo. Iraq began oil sales on December 10.
Rasheed said the U.N. embargo had drifted away from its original purpose and all reasons that had required its presence had now been removed.
"The embargo is totally unfair now...," he said.
Turkey and Iraq began joint economic meetings in Ankara earlier in the day to boost bilateral trade which has slumped to $200 million a year since the embargo took effect from about $2 billion.
According to the natural gas plan, Turkey's state oil and gas producer Turkish Petroleum (TPAO), state pipeline company Botas and Iraq would jointly begin exploring gas fields in Iraq, Kutas said.
The output from the fields would be pumped to Turkey through a 1,800-km (1,125-mile) pipeline, whose route is yet to be detailed at the continuing joint meetings in Ankara.
Kutan said Turkey would initially get three to four billion cubic metres of gas a year from Iraq through the pipeline and the amount would be raised to 10 billion cubic metres later.
"When the embargo is lifted, there are plans to link Qatari and Iraqi gas to Western markets through Turkey," he said.
Rasheed, who represents Iraq at the joint economic commission meetings in Ankara, met Turkish State Minister Ahmet Cemil Tunc, who is in charge of Iraqi affairs.
"We are aiming to raise the trade volume to at least pre-Gulf crisis levels of $2 to $3 billion a year," Tunc said.

The two ministers agreed to set up a second crossing near the existing Habur border gate to ease passage of Turkish trucks, which carry food items to northern Iraq under U.N. auspices and bring back cheaper Iraqi diesel.
"Talks are being held to build a second road passage of 25 km (15 miles)-long through the Hezil river in 1997," Tunc said in a statement.
He said the second road as well as the 24-hour operation of the Habur crossing would raise the number of trucks travelling to and from Iraq to a daily 5,000 from 500.
Turkey says it has lost about $27 billion in trade with Iraq since the Gulf crisis, before which Iraq was Turkey's third largest trade partner and top oil supplier.

A Turkish industry ministry circular said on Wednesday that the allowed amount of Iraqi diesel on Turkish trucks would raised to four to eight tonnes from two to 2.5 tonnes, depending on the type of the truck.
Turkey plans to sell sugar, pulses and detergent to Iraq for Baghdad's purchases of humanitarian goods under the U.N. deal, and has begun buying Iraqi crude oil at 75,000 barrels per day.
